text:
This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People trigger each other and learn lessons, and sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I’m pretty conservative about this, so I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on, you’re not ready.

You don’t have to be completely healed, but the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you, and responsible enough to deal with an actual child if sex creates one. If you can’t be a parent in either sense, you aren’t ready to date.

A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you’re least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good. Whether you should be in one depends on what you and the other person are ready for and have the resources for. Here’s a video that can help understand the long process.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")?
